title: Regression, correlation and biometrics: Galton/Pearson measurement program and Mendelian conflict
pressure: Biologists studying heredity/evolution faced continuous variation, noisy measurements and large family/population data. Statistical representations promised compression and comparison, but the meaning of correlation/regression depended on what was measured, how traits were defined and whether aggregate relations corresponded to biological mechanisms.
preExistingWorldModel: Galton developed quantitative anthropometry, regression toward the mean and correlation-like ideas from heredity data. Pearson formalized correlation, regression, goodness-of-fit/chi-square and biometric research infrastructure. Around 1900 Mendelian inheritance returned as a competing explanatory framework emphasizing discrete factors and experimental crosses.
candidateRoutes: treat statistical regularities as causal biological laws
use statistical summaries as descriptive/evaluative representations while keeping mechanism unresolved
observationsAndInstruments: Galton collected large anthropometric/family datasets and developed regression/correlation representations for heredity and variation.
Pearson extended/formalized these methods and built a durable Department/Biometric Laboratory research program with shared datasets, calculations and publications.
Contemporary correspondence shows active work on spurious correlation, definitions and criticism rather than automatic trust in coefficients.

Bateson and other Mendelians challenged biometric interpretations; a 1900 Royal Society referee report explicitly argued that Pearson's claim of an objectively existing average homotypic correlation rested on a fallacy.
Pearson–Bateson correspondence from 1901–03 records disagreements over Mendel, experiments and the relation between mathematical methods and biological statements.
The historical program was also tied to eugenics, demonstrating that technically sophisticated measurement can support ethically and scientifically defective inference/policy.
decisiveTests: A coefficient had to remain stable/interpretable under well-defined measurement/population choices rather than be treated as a property independent of construction.
Spurious-correlation cases tested whether a mathematical relation could arise from representation/selection rather than biological dependence.
Experimental crosses supplied materially different evidence about inheritance mechanisms than population correlations.
A good predictive/summary statistic did not automatically establish causal mechanism or legitimate policy inference.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Statistics became reusable scientific infrastructure for biological/population data, but its power made representation design itself a causal-risk surface. Quantification increased observability and compression while creating new opportunities to reify metrics as natural entities.
rivalsAndFailures: Biometric and Mendelian programs were serious rivals and later became partially synthesized rather than one simply disappearing.
Correlation could be mathematically correct yet biologically misleading if traits/populations/denominators were badly defined.
A referee could challenge whether a statistic had objective existence in nature even when calculations were correct.
The eugenics program is a major negative control: more measurement/statistics did not guarantee sound causal, normative or policy conclusions.
Mendelian discreteness did not make continuous biometric variation irrelevant; later quantitative genetics required both.
diffusionAndScaling: Correlation/regression/goodness-of-fit methods spread widely across science, social research and later industry. Statistical departments/laboratories made quantitative analysis a durable profession/institution.
standardsAndInstitutions: UCL statistical/biometric laboratories, Royal Society refereeing and journals provided durable data/method/evaluation infrastructure. Funding and disciplinary communities shaped which representations were stabilized.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Biometric/eugenic measurement supported coercive discriminatory ideologies/policies; this demonstrates that metaproductive measurement capability and net social value are separate axes.
secondOrderEffects: Modern statistical science gained powerful reusable tools, while later causal inference/experimental design had to address limitations of observational association and metric construction.
sourceNativeSummary: Galton/Pearson is not a simple story that quantification replaces subjective biology. Statistical representations dramatically increased scientific capability, but contemporary critics already attacked reification and spurious correlation; Mendelian experiments challenged mechanism inference, and eugenics shows that powerful measurement can amplify bad world models as well as good ones.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: Which biometric–Mendelian disputes were primarily empirical versus semantic/model-definition conflicts?
How much did eugenic goals shape variable selection and interpretation versus later misuse of otherwise general statistical tools?
